title: The third group: the biggest one
goal: Read and build third-declension nouns by relying on the "of" form, including neuter nouns and the i-stem subgroup.
bekal: find a third-declension stem from its "of" form
build all six forms of *rex*, *nomen* and *urbs*
recognize third-declension words in a sentence even when the subject form is unpredictable

dialogs.title: Colloquium — De regibus antiquis
dialogs.intro: A history lesson. Titus tells the story of Rome's first kings, and the pupils have lots of questions.

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.id: Today we're talking about the ancient kings.

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: De Numa. Numa rex bonus in fabulis est.
lines.id: About Numa. In the stories, Numa is a good king.
lines.literal: about Numa-about. Numa king good-masc in story-pl-in is-he.

lines.speaker: Lydia:
lines.text: Estne rex in urbe nostra hodie?
lines.id: Is there a king in our city today?
lines.literal: is-Q king in city-in our-in today?

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: Minime! Romani reges non amant. Nunc consules urbem regunt.
lines.id: Certainly not! Romans don't like kings. Now the consuls govern the city.
lines.literal: not-at-all! Roman-pl king-pl-obj not love-they. now consul-pl city-obj rule-they.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: And the soldiers? Do the soldiers guard the city?

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: Ita. Milites urbem et cives servant.
lines.id: Yes. The soldiers guard the city and its citizens.
lines.literal: yes. soldier-pl city-obj and citizen-pl-obj guard-they.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.text: Magister, quid est nomen regis primi?
lines.id: Sir, what's the name of the first king?
lines.literal: teacher-call, what is-it name king-of first-of?

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: Nomen regis primi Romulus est. Romulus urbem condit.
lines.id: The first king's name is Romulus. Romulus founds the city.
lines.literal: name king-of first-of Romulus is-it. Romulus city-obj found-he.

lines.speaker: Lydia:
lines.id: And the sea? Do the Romans have ships?

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: Multas naves habent. Mare nostrum dicunt!
lines.id: They have lots of ships. They call the sea Mare Nostrum!
lines.literal: many-pl-obj ship-pl-obj have-they. sea our-neut say-they!

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: Mare Nostrum, our sea — that's a good name!

notes: **Rex, regis — you can't rely on the subject form.** The third declension is the biggest group, and its subject forms are the wildest: *rex*, *miles*, *nomen*, *urbs*, *corpus*, *homo*. What is regular is the **"of" form**, which always ends in *-is*. Every other form is built from it: drop the *-is* and what's left is the stem. *Regis* → stem *reg-*; *militis* → stem *milit-*; *nominis* → stem *nomin-*. English often borrows the stem, not the subject form: *regal*, *military*, *nominal*.

**Mare nostrum — nostrum, not noster.** *Mare* is neuter, so its possessive wears the neuter outfit. This is the name Romans really used for the Mediterranean, and it wasn't empty boasting: by the first century its entire coastline lay within one empire.

**Urbe, urbem, urbs — three faces of one word.** Follow the stem: *urbs, urbis* → stem *urb-*, then *urbem* (object), *urbe* (with/in), *urbis* (of). It's the short, compact subject form that misleads you; the rest is straightforward. (English *urban* comes from the stem.)

**Reges non amant — why the Romans hated the word "king".** The Roman Republic was born by driving out the last king, and for five hundred years afterward *rex* was an accusation, not a title. Even Caesar refused to be called *rex*. That's why the word "king" all but vanished from Roman political language.

sections.title: The third declension: find the stem in the "of" form

blocks.text: The third group contains more words than groups one and two combined, including some of the most frequent words in all of Latin: *rex*, *lex*, *pax*, *homo*, *tempus*, *corpus*, *nomen*, *urbs*, *mater*, *pater*. They all use one and the same table.

Notice that masculine and feminine use exactly the same endings. In this group you can't guess the gender from the form at all — *rex* is masculine, *vox* feminine, and both follow an identical pattern. All you can rely on is the dictionary and the adjective that goes with the noun.

blocks.title: A working rule to make a habit
items: Look at the "of" form in the dictionary: *miles, milit**is***. Drop the *-is*. The stem is *milit-*.
Neuter words have two fixed peculiarities: subject and object are always twins, and the plural always ends in *-a*. This holds in every declension, so it's nothing new.
If the subject form is very short — *rex*, *lex*, *pax*, *nox*, *dux* — there's almost certainly a letter hidden in the stem: *reg-*, *leg-*, *pac-*, *noct-*, *duc-*.

blocks.text: A set of third-declension words slips in an *i* in two places: the plural "of" form becomes *-ium* and, for neuter words, the "with/in" form becomes *-i* and the plural *-ia*. This small subgroup is called the i-stems.

How to spot them: words whose subject and "of" forms have the same number of syllables (*civis, civis*; *nubes, nubis*), and words whose stem ends in two consonants (*urbs, urbis*; *pars, partis*; *mons, montis*). For beginners, it's enough to remember that the plural "of" form is *-ium*; everything else matches the main table.

Neuter words ending in *-e*, *-al* and *-ar* always belong to this group: *mare* (sea), *animal* (animal), *exemplar* (model). Their plurals are *maria*, *animalia*, *exemplaria* — which is where *Animalia*, the name biologists still use for the animal kingdom, comes from.
Always learn them in pairs: the subject form and the "of" form. Without the second one, you can't build anything.

Notice the deceptive *-us* pattern in the right-hand column: *corpus*, *tempus*, *opus*, *genus* are all **neuter** and belong to the third declension, not the second. Their "of" forms give them away: *corporis*, *temporis*, *operis*, *generis*. Their plurals are *corpora*, *tempora*, *opera*, *genera* — and English borrowed several of those plural forms just as they are.
